name: Majeed syndrome
aliases: chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis with congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia

reference.source: Textbook of Autoinflammation / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A recessive autoinflammatory disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in LPIN2, encoding the lipid-regulating enzyme lipin-2
Classic triad is chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, and a neutrophilic dermatosis
Bone disease begins in early childhood with recurrent painful, sterile inflammatory bone lesions and periosteal reaction
The anaemia is microcytic and dyserythropoietic, sometimes requiring transfusion, and reflects abnormal red cell production
Skin involvement typically resembles Sweet syndrome (neutrophilic dermatosis) or pustulosis
Growth impairment and recurrent fevers accompany the bone and marrow disease
Interleukin-1 blockade is generally more effective than tumour necrosis factor inhibition and can control the inflammatory features
reference.pathophysiology: Majeed syndrome results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in LPIN2, which encodes lipin-2, an enzyme involved in lipid metabolism and control of inflammation. Deficiency of lipin-2 dysregulates lipid handling in myeloid cells and enhances inflammasome activation, leading to excess interleukin-1 production. This drives sterile neutrophilic inflammation in bone (chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis) and skin, while associated effects on erythropoiesis produce a congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia. The central role of interleukin-1 explains the therapeutic benefit of IL-1 blockade.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs and MRI for multifocal osteomyelitis and periosteal reaction
Full blood count and blood film showing microcytic dyserythropoietic anaemia
Skin biopsy of neutrophilic dermatosis lesions
redFlags: Extensive bone involvement causing deformity or growth arrest
Failure to thrive with persistent systemic inflammation
Development of complications from chronic transfusion such as iron overload
reference.prognosis: Majeed syndrome is a chronic disease of childhood; with interleukin-1 blockade the inflammatory bone and skin disease can be well controlled, though anaemia and growth effects may persist and require additional support.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent bone lesions as infective osteomyelitis with prolonged antibiotics
Overlooking the associated anaemia as unrelated iron deficiency
Choosing tumour necrosis factor inhibition when interleukin-1 blockade is generally more effective
Failing to test for LPIN2 in a child with CRMO and unexplained anaemia
management: Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra or canakinumab is the disease-specific mainstay and controls the inflammatory bone and skin disease
Corticosteroids for acute flares, with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs providing only limited benefit for the bone pain
Management of the congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia with iron-appropriate care and red-cell transfusion when required
Symptomatic treatment of the neutrophilic dermatosis and analgesia for the painful osteomyelitic bone lesions
Growth monitoring and nutritional support given the associated growth impairment
Surveillance of acute-phase reactants, blood counts and imaging to track disease activity and treatment response
Multidisciplinary paediatric rheumatology, haematology and genetics care, with counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive LPIN2 disorder
